metadata.title: From Phone Trees to Chatbots: What Actually Changed
metadata.register: Conversational-Balanced (custom tone/voice per explicit user request — not the house Teardown register)
metadata.note: cli-explainer build reel. Through-line: build a keyword-matching support bot (v1, the old phone-tree style), test it, then revise it into an intent+urgency-aware bot (v2). Both scripts are real and were actually run to capture the OUTPUT beats' transcripts — not invented. v2 is explicitly disclosed in narration as a simplified heuristic stand-in for a trained NLU/LLM system, not a real one — avoids overclaiming (DOUBLE-CHECK LAW). channel handle set to @HumanitariansAI per user request (v2 revision).

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — ask shown answered
beats.narration_text: Here's a question worth sitting with: when your support call gets picked up by a bot instead of a person, what actually changed? Let's not just talk about it — let's build both versions and watch them handle the same three messages.

props.command: claude "show me, with real code, what actually changes when a company swaps its phone-tree support bot for an AI chatbot"
output: 1 of 3 test messages stumped the old one

beats.role_note: presenter intro + one-line video summary — added per user request
beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Agrima. This video looks at what actually changes when a company swaps an old rule-based support bot for a modern AI chatbot — why companies make the switch, and where the tradeoffs still show up.
beats.visual_intent: simple presenter card: name, then a one-line summary of what the video covers

beats.role_note: the why, before any code — SHOW, not a bare card
beats.narration_text: Companies aren't swapping in chatbots because it's trendy — three plain reasons: cost, always-on availability, instant response. One bot serves thousands of conversations for a fraction of the price, never clocks out, replies in seconds. Real reasons. Whether it's actually GOOD at the conversation is what we're testing.
beats.visual_intent: three-column card: Cost / 24/7 Availability / Instant Response, each with a one-line explanation, appearing in sequence

beats.narration_text: Let's ask Claude for the version most people mean by “chatbot” in, say, 2015: a script that just matches keywords — a phone tree you type into instead of press buttons on.

props.command:
claude "write support_bot_v1.py — an old-style keyword-matching support bot, like a phone tree.
  Test it on 3 real support messages."

beats.narration_text: Here's what it actually does. Every rule is just: does the message contain this exact word? If none of the rules match, it falls back to a generic phone-tree menu. That's the whole bot — no understanding, just string matching.

props.title: support_bot_v1.py
props.code:
# support_bot_v1.py — Claude Code output
RULES = [
    (["password", "reset", "locked out"],
     "To reset your password, go to Settings > Security > Reset Password."),
    (["refund", "money back"],
     "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days."),
    (["hours", "open"],
     "Our support hours are Mon-Fri, 9am-6pm EST."),
]
FALLBACK = "Sorry, I didn't understand. Press 1 for billing, 2 for account, 3 for a human."

def respond(message):
    text = message.lower()
    for keywords, reply in RULES:
        if any(k in text for k in keywords):   # <- exact word match only
            return reply
    return FALLBACK
props.sparkLine: If the word's not there, it's not there.

beats.role_note: OPEN vox slot → Manim, the REAL captured transcript
beats.narration_text: Run it on three real messages. Password reset, matched. Refund request, matched. But the third — “charged twice by mistake, I'm really upset” — no exact keyword lines up, so it falls through to the generic menu. It isn't wrong, exactly — it never learned to read the sentence, only to scan for magic words.
beats.visual_intent: chat-bubble transcript of the 3 test messages and the bot's real replies; the 3rd exchange visually flagged MISSED

beats.narration_text: So let's fix the actual gap. Ask Claude to update the bot so it responds to the MEANING of a message, not just one exact phrase — and to notice when someone sounds upset enough that a human should step in.

props.command:
claude "update support_bot_v1.py:
  -> match on the MEANING/intent of a message,
     not one exact phrase (a family of related signals)
  -> detect when a message is urgent/emotional enough
     to hand off to a human agent
  -> re-test on the SAME 3 messages"

beats.narration_text: Here's the revision. Each intent now has a family of related signals — “password”, “reset”, “locked out” point the same way. A second check runs alongside it: does this sound urgent? If so, it adds a human handoff. A simplified stand-in for a real trained model — but the shape holds: read for meaning, know your limits.

props.title: support_bot_v2.py
props.code:
# support_bot_v2.py — Claude Code output (revision)
INTENTS = {
  "refund": {"signals": ["refund", "money back",
              "charged twice", "overcharged"],
             "reply": "Refunds are processed within 5-7 business days."},
  # ...reset_password, hours defined the same way
}
ESCALATE_SIGNALS = ["upset", "angry", "unacceptable", "mistake", "furious"]

def respond(message):
    text = message.lower()
    best_intent = best_match(text, INTENTS)      # <- scores signal FAMILIES
    urgent = any(s in text for s in ESCALATE_SIGNALS)
    reply = INTENTS[best_intent]["reply"] if best_intent else None
    if urgent:
        reply = (reply or "") + " Connecting you with a human agent now."
    return reply or "Can you rephrase, or say 'agent' for a human?"
props.sparkLine: Read the intent, not the word.

beats.role_note: OPEN vox slot → Manim, the REAL captured transcript
beats.narration_text: Same three messages, new bot. Password and refund land the same as before. But the third now matches “refund” through “charged twice”, AND catches “upset” and “mistake” as urgency signals — so it answers AND flags a human to step in. Nothing about the message changed. What changed is what the bot was built to notice.
beats.visual_intent: the SAME chat transcript, now with all 3 exchanges landing; the 3rd flagged UNDERSTOOD + escalated

beats.role_note: the lesson, stated plainly — no hype
beats.narration_text: Here's the honest version. The new bot got better at reading meaning, not just words — and better at knowing when to step back. Real progress. Not the whole story: complex or emotional situations still need a person, edge cases still slip through, and trust isn't automatic — it's built one good conversation at a time, or lost the same way.
beats.visual_intent: OLD vs NEW recap cards side by side, then a 'still true either way' tradeoffs line: complex/emotional issues, edge cases, trust

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — prompt read aloud AND discussed
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Try this: pick a real conversation your team has had with a customer — an easy one and a messy one — and ask Claude to sketch out where a bot should confidently handle it, and exactly where it should hand off to a person instead. That line is the actual design decision companies are making right now.

props.command:
claude "here are two real customer messages — [an easy one] and
  [a messy one]. For each: should a chatbot handle this alone,
  or hand off to a human? What specific signal in the message
  tells you that?"

beats.role_note: OUTRO LAW — title restate, last beat
beats.narration_text: From Phone Trees to Chatbots — what actually changed. Cost, availability, and speed are why companies switched. Understanding intent, and knowing when to step back, is what separates a good bot from an annoying one.
